Data Collection

Initial QAQC of raw data
Using Docker for QAQC Using Docker is kind of having an apartment in an apartment building. The Docker image/template is built and users are able to use a container to work in. So the image is like the building and the container is like an apartment in the building. Users share the kernel (likened to plumbing in the example), but they have their own way to get in. The important thing to remember is that any changes made in a container are temporary.

title: FEAT Wet Lab Field Guide
text:
A main species of focus for the Fisheries Engineering and Acoustic Technologies (FEAT) group is Pacific hake (Merluccius productus), also known as Pacific whiting. A standing biennial survey is conducted jointly with Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) to estimate the biomass and assess the distribution of the West coast population. This particular survey, as well as other surveys and research conducted by the group, uses an Integrated Acoustic and Trawl (IAT) approach.
(insert hake photo)
An IAT survey uses a combination of data collected from acoustic transducers (backscatter) and biological data from trawls. The catch data provides groundtruthing, while the specimen data provides length frequency and age information to characterize the size composition of the target species. Unlike some surveys, the locations for the trawls are not set in advance. Trawls are adaptive, depending on the pattern of observed backscatter layers.
(photo of acoustics reading?)
This document compiles information to set up, work in, and tear down the wet lab aboard NOAA research vessels, and should provide enough information to adapt to other platforms. This serves as an overview of the wet lab personnel responsibilities, provides details to complete the cruise safely and efficiently, and outlines collection protocols. Cruise specific protocols are contained in the separate wet lab materials available in the wet lab.

title: Responsibilities and Expectations
text:
You represent NOAA both on the ship and in port

Regardless of whether you are a NOAA employee, contractor, or volunteer, you should conduct yourself appropriately

You are responsible for yourself

While teamwork is key to a successful survey, the most effective teams are built on trust and accountability. Be accountable for your actions, both while on shift and off. Obey the standing orders of the ship and be courteous to your fellow shipmates.

Be available and ready for all duties

Because of the adaptive nature of the survey, time in between wet lab duties can vary. Work with lab leads and/or the acoustics lab to stay in touch during these times so you can be available at a moment’s notice for either a tow or other relevant duties.
The lab lead(s) must remain in contact with the acoustics lab while on shift. Let them know where you will be and carry a radio if necessary.

Work together to complete cruise objectives

In order to accomplish the varied tasks on the survey, everyone must work together. There can also be a lot of downtime so sharing the duties outside of the lab can help to keep busy.

Follow established sampling protocols

It is important to follow the established sampling protocols to ensure continuity between shifts, legs, and cruises. The lab lead(s) will provide a walkthrough and review of protocols at the start of each leg. Don’t hesitate to ask questions; it benefits the whole team when everyone is on the same page.

Be diligent to collect the best quality data

It is easy to become distracted when doing repetitive tasks. Changing jobs frequently and moving around to different stations can help.
Always check to make sure a species is not on the Special Sampling list before tossing. These change from cruise to cruise so please be familiar with lab document locations. Special Sampling lists will be available near the main computer in the wet lab. The lab lead(s) also have access to these species in CLAMS.

Maintain supplies and equipment

Keep equipment clean and in working order. Let the wet lab lead know if you notice any supplies getting low.

title: Responsibilities and Expectations
text:
Duty Priorities

Collecting catch and sample data

While there may be other duties to work on throughout the cruise, the first priority is collecting the catch and sample data. If other duties require attention while sorting and processing is still going on in the lab, work with the acousticians who can either take care of the project or they can take someone’s place in the wet lab.
Note that during towing operations, NO DUMPING is allowed to minimize the possibility of recapture. As soon as the net is in the water, all dumping must cease. This is also the case for any stationary CTD stations, zooplankton net tows, Methot net tows, etc.

Prepare sensors, cameras, etc. to deploy on the net (also called ‘peripheral devices’ in this document)

It doesn’t take long to get sensors and other peripheral equipment ready to put onto the net. The survey tech will take care of the equipment maintained by the ship (such as the FS70), but the wet lab staff and volunteers should take care of getting the temperature and depth unit(s) ready for deployment, as well as any cameras or other peripheral equipment.
Be prepared to go out on deck by donning required personal protective equipment (PPE).

Help with Marine Mammal watches, when possible

Mammal watches before towing operations (and in some cases during) are required. If it isn’t interfering with catch processing, the wet lab staff and volunteers will need to help cover the watch so the fisher can focus on their duties. More often than not, the wet lab lead(s) will not be available for the start of the marine mammal watch due to the preparation of peripheral devices.

Retrieve sensors, cameras, etc. from the net

The survey tech will take care of retrieving the sensors maintained by the ship. Check with the lab lead(s) or chief scientist what the current protocol is for retrieving FEAT maintained equipment. If you are allowed on deck, you must go out with required PPE (hardhat, PFD - personal flotation device).

Maintain data from peripheral equipment

Data should be downloaded from the equipment and stored in the appropriate place as soon as possible to ensure that the equipment is in working order before sending it out again.

Keep lab clean between tows

Most of the time, there is another shift, another group, or another science center sharing the wet lab. A good rinse to knock down any fish goo, livers, blood, and other nasties is required after every tow. It’s easier to clean it when it’s fresh instead of waiting until it cakes on. Always clean the lab like it is the last tow of the day to ensure the other shift/group has a clean working environment.

Deep clean lab after every leg

After the last tow for the leg, a deep clean needs to be done to clean nooks and crannies to free any smelly debris. Simple green is provided (and the ship should have some as well) as well as scrub brushes and sponges in the cleaning bucket. More information on required areas to clean later in the document.

Deep, deep clean after cruise – See the cleaning sheet for details.

title: Responsibilities and Expectations
section: Keeping Busy Outside of Sampling Duties
text:
Keeping Busy Outside of Sampling Duties
The lab lead(s) may assign other sampling duties outside the wet lab as well as other duties for the current cruise. If you would like something to do, talk with either the lead(s) or the Chief Scientist.

title: Ship Safety
text:
When you’re in port (before, in between, or after a leg of the cruise) it is important to familiarize yourself with potential tsunami evacuation routes depending on where you are.
Before you go on a planned outing, familiarize yourself with where you will be on the map and the best route for evacuation.
Potential threats from a tsunami can vary drastically, so a little planning can go a long way to ensure the safety of oneself, and those around you.
Maps are provided below for common ports. Make note of the docking location for the ship.
Links are also provided for an online version of each port’s tsunami evacuation map.


Newport, OR Tsunami EvacuationSan Francisco, CA Tsunami EvacuationSeattle, WA Tsunami Evacuation



The map below is separated into Newport-North and Newport-South, with the Newport-North map for when you are north of the Yaquina Bay Bridge, and Newport-South for when you are south of the bridge.
The ORANGE regions on the map represent the area that must be evacuated if there is a distant tsunami, in which the earthquake occurs far from the Oregon Coast.
The YELLOW regions on the map represent the area that must be evacuated if there is a local Cascadia earthquake and tsunami that occurs on the Oregon Coast.
The GREEN regions on the map represent the area that is outside the hazard area. Evacuate to the green if you there is a tsunami warning, if you feel an earthquake, OR if you are unsure about the risk for any reason.
Remain in the evacuation zone until you are notified by authorities that it is safe to leave
This link will take you to the same maps seen below. It will allow you to zoom in to identify where you are and evacuation areas around you.














The map below does not provide as much detail as the Newport, OR map.
The link below will take you to the same map that is interactive. This allows you to identify your location and evacuation areas around you in greater detail than the map.
Wherever you might be in San Francisco, you will be less than 10 blocks from a safe area should a Tsunami occur.
The YELLOW on the map represents a tsunami hazard area and should be evacuated if you feel an earthquake, if you are given a tsunami warning, OR if you are unsure of the situation.
The GREEN on the map represents safe evacuation locations.
As San Francisco is a large city, if a localized earthquake/tsunami event were to occur, you should be aware of the dangers associated with evacuating to an area that has large buildings and other vulnerable structures.
Refer to this link for a much more detailed, interactive map to plan your safe evacuation route.

(insert SanFran map?)



Due to the terrain in and around Seattle, you are not far from safety should an earthquake/tsunami occur.
The map on the next page provides a different look at the tsunami hazard zones in Seattle. This map was created to show the potential levels of inundation from a tsunami associated with an earthquake along the Seattle Fault. As you can see, areas that have an inlet or cove represent the highest threat of inundation from a tsunami.
The GREEN on the map represents areas where inundation from a tsunami could be 0-0.5 meters. The YELLOW on the map represents areas where inundation from a tsunami could be 0.5-2.0 meters. The ORANGE on the map represents areas where inundation from a tsunami could be 2.0-5.0 meters.
While this map doesn’t actually show you where to go if a tsunami were to occur, it is an important reference depicting areas to avoid should an event occur. Should an earthquake, tsunami warning, or uncertainty involving an earthquake/tsunami occur, your first priority is to head for higher ground.
Follow this link to find out more information about a potential earthquake/tsunami in Seattle.

(Insert seattle map?)
